reference.source: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: Defined histologically by a thickened subepithelial collagen band beneath the surface epithelium accompanied by a lamina propria inflammatory infiltrate
A paediatric or young-adult pattern typically presents with abdominal pain and iron-deficiency anaemia and is often confined to the stomach
An adult pattern more often accompanies chronic watery diarrhoea and overlaps with collagenous colitis and other microscopic colitides
Endoscopy may show a nodular or mosaic mucosa, erosions, or an essentially normal-appearing stomach, so diagnosis rests on biopsy
There is a recognised association with coeliac disease, so duodenal sampling and coeliac serology are worthwhile
Entrapment of surface epithelium and dilated capillaries within the collagen band helps distinguish it from other gastritides
No definitive therapy exists; management is empirical and supportive, including iron repletion and trials of acid suppression or corticosteroids
reference.pathophysiology: Collagenous gastritis is a rare disorder in which an abnormally thick, patchy band of subepithelial collagen is deposited immediately beneath the gastric surface epithelium, associated with a chronic inflammatory infiltrate in the lamina propria and often entrapped dilated capillaries and detached surface cells. The mechanism is uncertain but is presumed to reflect an aberrant reparative or immune-mediated response of the subepithelial fibroblast sheath, mirroring the process seen in collagenous colitis, with which it may coexist. The abnormal mucosa can bleed and impair nutrient handling, contributing to the iron-deficiency anaemia commonly seen in affected children and young adults.
additionalDifferentials: Collagenous colitis or collagenous sprue as part of a diffuse gastrointestinal process
additionalInvestigations: Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with multiple gastric biopsies, using special stains to highlight the subepithelial collagen band
Duodenal biopsies and coeliac serology to detect coexisting coeliac disease
Colonoscopy with biopsies where diarrhoea suggests coexisting microscopic (collagenous) colitis
Full blood count and iron studies to characterise anaemia
Helicobacter pylori testing to exclude a treatable co-factor
Nutritional and coeliac-related deficiency screening where malabsorption is suspected
redFlags: Significant or refractory iron-deficiency anaemia requiring transfusion or intravenous iron
Marked weight loss or failure to thrive in children
Severe or dehydrating diarrhoea in the adult diarrhoeal pattern
reference.prognosis: The condition tends to be chronic and relapsing; the subepithelial collagen band often persists on repeat biopsy, but symptoms can be controlled and serious complications are uncommon, with prognosis largely determined by associated coeliac or colonic disease.
pitfalls: Overlooking the diagnosis when the mucosa looks endoscopically normal and biopsies are not taken or not specially stained
Failing to search for coexisting coeliac disease or collagenous colitis
Attributing the iron-deficiency anaemia solely to another cause and missing the gastric source
Confusing the entrapped surface changes with a neoplastic process
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
